When you build tools that let an LLM agent query data, the database choice stops being an architecture-slide decision and becomes a failure-mode decision: what happens when the model does something reasonable-sounding but slow, or generates DDL that quietly does not work. I benchmarked that question the slow way — a 14-benchmark suite behind the duckdb-mcp server, measuring everything from DDL speed to MCP round-trip overhead. The numbers argued for DuckDB, and the gotchas were worth the exercise by themselves.

The numbers that changed my defaults

All figures below come from the project's benchmark suite (test_benchmarks.py and the integration tests that pin each practice), run against DuckDB CLI v1.5.4. One machine: 8-core laptop, NVMe, DuckDB 1.5.4 (Variegata) defaults, single run, warm cache. Treat the ratios as the finding and the absolutes as indicative.

Bulk insert: generate_series, never INSERT VALUES. 100,000 users land in 27 ms via a select-from-generate_series. Hand the same task to a model's natural instinct — long INSERT INTO ... VALUES (...), (...) lists — and you are paying parse costs per statement, and the practice guide's rule of thumb is to stop generating them past a thousand rows anyway.

Parquet as the ingest format, not CSV. Parquet files came in around 27% of the equivalent CSV size, and read_parquet queries the file zero-copy without loading it into a database first. For agent pipelines this matters twice: smaller files mean faster handoffs between pipeline stages and cheaper multi-copy retention — files are what agents pass around, after all.

Cross-database joins are instant. Three attached databases of 100K rows each joined in 8 ms. One caveat that cost me an hour: ATTACH needs a path within reach of the session doing the attaching (attached :memory: databases, for what it is worth, do join fine within a single v1.5.4 session), and every CLI invocation is a fresh session — so anything doing cross-process cross-DB work still means temp files, which the server does for you.

Window functions scale flat-ish. ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD, running sums and NTILE at 100K rows all landed in a uniform 6.9–7.5 ms band. The kind of analysis an agent is most likely to be asked for is exactly what columnar engines are boringly good at.

JSON output is affordable. The CLI's -json mode adds 9–15% overhead versus plain text. For machine-readable tool responses, that is a tax worth paying — but see the coercion post, because the JSON types need re-hydration.

The failure you will only find at runtime

Here is the one the documentation under-sells: on DuckDB v1.5.4, DEFAULT, UNIQUE, CHECK and FOREIGN KEY constraints all work fine. IDENTITY fails with Constraint not implemented!. SERIAL fails earlier, at parse time: v1.5.4 has no SERIAL type at all (Catalog Error: Type with name SERIAL does not exist!). Any model trained on Postgres-heavy corpora will generate SERIAL PRIMARY KEY on demand, all day, and every one of those calls dies.

The fix belongs below the prompt, at the tool level:

CREATE SEQUENCE user_id_seq;
CREATE TABLE users (
  id BIGINT DEFAULT nextval('user_id_seq') PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT UNIQUE CHECK (email LIKE '%@%')
);

Auto-increment through CREATE SEQUENCE + nextval() works and keeps the IDs in the database, where they belong — the practice notes are blunt about it: never generate IDs in Python, use DuckDB-native bulk patterns. Because the MCP server exposes schema creation through recipes that already use the working pattern, the model never gets the chance to discover the failure at 3 a.m. on someone's pipeline.

Why this matters for agents specifically

An agent workflow is an unpredictable query generator with a budget. Three properties of DuckDB line up with that: it is a library-grade database that needs no server to administer (an agent can be handed a file path and be productive immediately), it is columnar and fast on exactly the analytical shapes models tend to write, and its failure modes are loud exceptions rather than silent plan degradations.

The benchmark suite is not an argument that DuckDB beats a warehouse for everything — 500K rows is not big data. It is an argument that for the agent-tooling niche — single-node files, sub-second interactive queries, Parquet in the middle, JSON out the other side — the boring choice is the database that lets your tools encode the three patterns that work (generate_series bulk insert, SEQUENCE auto-increment, Parquet ingest) and make the wrong ones impossible.
